angles.drive: You are better with a rival in sight. Your own pace never quite wakes you, so you measure yourself against a person rather than a plan. Pick your rivals on purpose, and you turn a reflex into the fastest way you grow.
angles.cost_self: Being better with rivals leaves you rarely at your best alone. Without someone to beat, you drift rather than push, so the goals only you care about wait longest. Find a rival for the private goals too, and you stop leaving your own for last.
angles.cost_others: Better with a rival, you turn a peer into one without asking. You would rather race someone than keep them company, and you hand a contest to a friend who wanted none. Name the race, and you give them the choice to run it.

angles.drive: You bet big because only a real stake gets all of you, and you would rather risk a lot on one move than a little on many. If you let small bets count too, you stop missing the gains that come slowly.
angles.cost_self: Where you bet big, you lose at the same size. You stake the whole amount instead of keeping some in reserve. When you hold back one part of each bet, you keep the savings a single loss would take.
angles.cost_others: On a shared stake, you bet someone else's year with your own. You would rather win it all for both of you than keep half safe, and their caution becomes your dare. Ask first, because you keep a partner who chose the risk.

angles.drive: With a win in hand, you would rather share the credit than keep it, because a prize means more with your people inside it. When a win can count before you have shared it, you get to enjoy it twice.
angles.cost_self: Taking the credit alone feels like showing off to you. You hand out credit rather than keep it, and your own work goes unnamed. If you put your own name on your part, you stop losing the chances that follow credit.
angles.cost_others: The credit you share lands on people who did not run for it. You would rather have company at the finish than stand there alone, and you pass out what only you earned. Name who did what, to give praise each person can use.

angles.drive: In new company, you are comparing before you have said much. A clear rank makes you feel safe, and you compare yourself to someone rather than get to know them. Once the ranking is done, you have often missed the person.
angles.cost_self: Always comparing gives you a result and never rest. You would rather know where you rank than enjoy where you are, so no win gets time to feel like one. You lose the quiet of a good week to a score only you can see.
angles.cost_others: Whenever a friend has good news, you compare before you say well done. You measure the gap ahead of being glad for them, and you give less praise than they earned. You can let their news stay theirs for a day and compare later.

angles.drive: You feel every loss as a blow to your standing. You would rather sit out a contest than risk losing it, because your standing feels at stake. Remember that you are beaten far less often than you think, and you keep every one.
angles.cost_self: Hating to lose costs you the losses that would have taught you most. You would rather not play than be beaten, and you never enter the contests with the most to teach you. You protect a record with very few wins on it.
angles.cost_others: Shared things turn into contests when you hate to lose. You would rather win the argument than keep the evening, and you put a friend on the losing side of a game they never entered. You leave with the point and a little less warmth.

angles.drive: As a contest gets close, you spend to win it. You would rather pay to stay ahead than risk falling behind, and you spend to prove a point. Ask yourself before you pay whether you want the thing or only the win.
angles.cost_self: Where you spend to win, you end up with the win and without the money. You would rather look ahead of a rival than quietly stay ahead, so the savings go on rounds nobody asked for. You notice the money you did not keep last.
angles.cost_others: To win, you spend what is not only yours. You would rather cover the whole bill than split it, and you spend money your partner set aside for the two of you. You spend the trust in a shared account faster than the balance.

angles.drive: Advancing is how your body answers the world: a foot in the door, a stake in the ground, a seat claimed at tables you were not quite invited to. You expand quietly and hold what you take. By the time anyone objects, you are already infrastructure.
angles.cost_self: The abandoned corner of the office became your project station one shelf at a time, over six unremarkable weeks. Nobody approved it and nobody could unwind it, since by then the whole team used it. Management eventually labeled it, which is how conquest gets certified.
angles.cost_others: People discover your influence the way surveyors discover fences: already installed, weathered in, slightly past the property line. Nobody remembers granting the territory, and everybody relies on how well you run it. Complaints tend to die out on the walk over.

angles.drive: Letting go is simply not in your body’s vocabulary. The application gets resubmitted, the door gets knocked on again, the no gets treated as a scheduling issue. What you grip, you keep gripping, well past the point where everyone else’s hands opened.
angles.cost_self: The permit was denied twice, and the third application had photographs, precedents, and a cover letter that quoted the inspector back to himself. It passed. The clerk who stamped it said, with respect, that they hoped never to see your name again.
angles.cost_others: Opponents budget extra rounds for you, because your first defeat is just your intake meeting. People who watched you lose in March have learned not to celebrate, since your Aprils have a reputation. Eventually the resistance factors you in like weather and yields early.

angles.drive: Pressure that bends other people mostly just settles your stance. Criticism, setbacks, the year everything went wrong: your posture after each one is level ground. You take the hit, absorb it, and stand where you stood, which is its own kind of answer.
angles.cost_self: The venture failed publicly, and you showed up Monday at the usual hour with an ordinary face and a revised plan. The people waiting to see you diminished waited all week. By Friday they were reading the plan, mostly to learn what standing back up looks like.
angles.cost_others: People stop testing you after the first time they watch a real blow land and change nothing. The steadiness reads as almost unfair. Behind your back, the description is always some version of the same sentence: whatever happens, that one stays standing.

angles.drive: Yours is a word your body enforces before your mind gets consulted. The parking spot, the project, the Sunday routine: incursions get met with a speed that surprises even you. Most of the invasions were imaginary. The defense spending has been extremely real.
angles.cost_self: A new hire touched your client file with good intentions, and the temperature of your reply preserved itself in the team’s memory for a year. They were trying to help. The help never came back, and now the workload is defended and entirely yours.
angles.cost_others: Colleagues navigate your territory with a map they keep updated among themselves: what not to touch, which chair is yours, when to ask versus announce. Cooperation with you has border-crossing paperwork. Some people just trade elsewhere, and you file that as respect.

angles.drive: You keep score with geological patience. The slight from 2019 is filed, cross-referenced, and quietly load-bearing in how you treat its author. Forgiveness feels like surrendering land. So the ledger grows, and you pay its storage costs nightly without auditing what the grudges rent.
angles.cost_self: You attended the wedding and were pleasant all evening to the cousin, who never knew that the seating, the small talk, and the early exit were all footnotes to a loan unreturned in 2017. It was sixty dollars. The interest is now a relationship.
angles.cost_others: People sense the ledger without seeing it. There is a slight tax in how you greet certain names, a coolness with fifteen-year-old foundations. Newcomers get warned in shorthand: do not end up in the book. Nobody can say exactly how one gets out of it.

angles.drive: When you want something, obstacles register as terrain rather than as people. The plan rolls forward, objections get graded flat, and you genuinely do not hear the crunch. Afterward the path is open and efficient, and someone behind you is holding pieces of their fence.
angles.cost_self: The family holiday got decided in one message, yours, sent before the poll you had proposed finished collecting votes. Three people had conflicts. The trip was excellent and efficiently run, and two of the three still bring up the poll, humorously, in a specific tone.
angles.cost_others: People agree with you in meetings and then meet again, smaller, without you. It is not sabotage. It is the only lane where their input survives contact. You keep winning the official votes and losing informal ones you never find out happened.
